newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Jordan airliner in Kuwait heralds rapprochement.
newsitem.headline: Jordan airliner in Kuwait heralds rapprochement.

text.p: A Jordanian aircraft landed in Kuwait on Thursday for the first time in seven years marking what diplomats saw as a new stage in the slow rapprochement with Iraq's friends.

"Six years ago it was almost unthinkable to see a Jordanian aircraft landing peacefully in Kuwait," a Western diplomat told Reuters. But, "there is still a long way ahead before ties can go back to normal".
Although the Royal Jordanian Airlines aircraft carried 142 travellers on the first of two schedueled weekly flights, Jordanians here say they still cannot obtain visas for friends back home.
Kuwait had downgraded ties and cut generous financial aid to several Arab states, including Jordan, which it accused of sympathising with Iraq during its 1990-91 occupation.

Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990 and annexed it for seven months before U.S.-led coalition forces liberated the tiny oil-rich state in 19911. Arabs were severely divided into a camp that opposed the Gulf War and another that supported the use of multinational forces.

About half a million Jordanians, Palestinians, Yemenis and Sudanese used to live in Kuwait before the occupation. Most of them fled during the war or were forced to leave after the liberation amid hostile feelings among Kuwaitis.
"Judging from recent indicators its seems that Kuwait's government has decided to open up for a gradual normalisation with these countries," another diplomat said.
In May Foreign Minister Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Sabah said he hopes ties with all Arab states except an Iraq ruled by Saddam Hussein would be improved.
Since the crisis Kuwait has snubbed many departures by Arab states whose economies suffered the loss of generous aid from the oil-rich state.
In recent weeks Kuwait's government debated with lawmakers the possibility of improving ties with some Arab states -- such as Jordan, Yemen and Sudan -- which appeared to back Iraq during the crisis.
Diplomats say such moves might lack public support although there are some within the government who strongly back it.

In an apparent ice breaking move the Emir Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah on Wednesday received a Sudanese minister who carried a message from President Omar Hassan al-Bashir, in the first contact on such a level since the crisis.
On the same day Yemen's President Ali Abduallah Saleh met in Sanaa with a team of Kuwaiti intellectuals, including two former ministers.
"Kuwait wants to drag these countries from Iraq's camp. To have them as friends is better than having them as friends of an enemy," said a diplmat.
